title: Triads on guitar string sets
description: Build close triads from pitch classes on adjacent strings. Do not memorize a grid first.

cards.back: The group of strings a voicing uses. For close three-note triads, start with three adjacent strings.

cards.front: What is this lesson’s goal — memorizing twelve shapes, or something else?
cards.back: Construction on the neck from notes. Generalized shape tables are optional after you can derive.

cards.front: List the four steps to place a triad on a chosen set.
cards.back: 1. Spell the triad. 2. Find those pitch classes on each string. 3. Pick one note per string in a compact span. 4. Name inversion from the lowest sounding note.

cards.front: Most adjacent open strings are a P4 (5 frets). What is G→B, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Strings 3→2 are a major 3rd (4 frets). A pattern that works on D–G–B is not a blind copy on G–B–E.

cards.front: What are the open notes on strings 4–3–2?
On strings 4–3–2 (frets 0–14), where is C? E? G?
Give compact C major voicings on 4–3–2 for all three inversions.
cards.back: Root 10 9 8 = C E G. First 14 12 13 or 2 0 1 = E G C. Second 5 5 5 = G C E.

cards.front: Check root-position C on 4–3–2 by counting from the opens.
Derive G major on 4–3–2 in all three inversions.
cards.back: Root 5 4 3 = G B D. First 9 7 8 = B D G. Second 0 0 0 or 12 12 12 = D G B.

cards.front: How do you turn a major triad into minor on the same set?
cards.back: Lower only the string that carries the third by one fret. Leave root and fifth.

cards.front: From C major on 4–3–2, make C minor in all three inversions.
cards.back: Root 10 8 8 (E on string 3 down). First 13 12 13 (E on string 4 down). Second 5 5 4 (E on string 2 down).

cards.front: Give C major on strings 5–4–3: root and first inversion. Opens are A D G.
cards.back: Root 3 2 0 = C E G. First 7 5 5 = E G C. Verify first: A+7=E, D+5=G, G+5=C.

cards.front: What is second-inversion C major on strings 5–4–3?
Which string sets share the same relative fret spacing? Which set does not?
cards.back: 6–5–4 matches 5–4–3 (both P4 gaps). 3–2–1 crosses the G–B break, so rebuild from notes.

cards.front: Place D major (D F♯ A) on strings 3–2–1 in all three inversions.
Name chord + inversion: 3 2 0 on 5–4–3; 9 7 8 on 4–3–2; 7 8 7 on 3–2–1.
cards.back: C major root; G major first; G major second (D G B).

cards.front: Melody note is G on top. Which C major inversion on 4–3–2 puts G highest?
cards.back: Root position 10 9 8 — top string fret 8 is G.

cards.front: Why does copying 5 5 5 from 4–3–2 onto 3–2–1 not give the same chord?
cards.back: Open-string intervals differ (G–B is a major 3rd), so the same frets stack different pitch classes.

cards.front: How do you name the inversion of a constructed voicing?
cards.back: From the lowest sounding note (bass), not from a shape nickname.
